incumbent.name: Wendy McNamara
incumbent.summary: Wendy McNamara, an Evansville Republican, has represented House District 76 since 2010 and chairs the House Courts and Criminal Code Committee {caucus_mcnamara}. She directs EVSC Early College for the Evansville Vanderburgh School Corporation {caucus_mcnamara} {evpl_guide}.
record: Chairs the Courts and Criminal Code Committee and serves on Roads and Transportation, per the House Republican caucus {caucus_mcnamara}. In August 2026 she chaired the interim study committees on Public Health, Behavioral Health and Human Services and on Corrections and Criminal Code {caucus_interim}.
April 10, 2025: Voted yes on SEA 1, the 2025 property-tax law (passed 65-29) {rc_sea1_433}. April 25, 2025: Voted yes on the 2025 budget (HEA 1001), adopted 66-27 {rc_hb1001_576}.

Dec. 5, 2025: Voted yes on HB 1032, the mid-decade congressional redistricting bill, which passed the House 57-41 {rc_hb1032_28}. She told WNIN she would vote the same way again, citing concern about federal funding for Posey and Vanderburgh counties: "I wasn't willing to make that risk of not supporting that" {wnin_hd76}.
Jan. 28, 2026: Voted yes on HB 1002, the 2026 electric utility affordability bill (passed 89-4) {rc_hb1002_149}; she called it "a big step forward" {wnin_hd76}.

2026 session: Authored HEA 1116, which prohibits cryptocurrency kiosks statewide; she said "These kiosks are a tool bad actors use to target seniors" {caucus_crypto}. Authored HEA 1303, which creates a separate code section for child sexual abuse material offenses, a new distribution crime and higher felony levels {caucus_csam}.

Earlier laws the caucus lists as hers include juvenile justice reform (2022), a competency-to-stand-trial bill (HB 1238, 2024) and trucker training on spotting human trafficking (HEA 1196, 2023) {caucus_mcnamara}. She told WNIN that juvenile justice reform is the work she is proudest of {wnin_hd76}.

race_context: House District 76 covers all of Posey County and part of Vanderburgh County {caucus_mcnamara}, including Evansville's west side, Mount Vernon, New Harmony and Poseyville, with about 65,000 constituents {wnin_hd76}.
McNamara is seeking a ninth term; WNIN reports no Democrat has held the seat since 2008 {wnin_hd76}. She was reelected without opposition in 2024 {wiki_2026}.
Both McNamara and Logan Patberg were unopposed for their parties' nominations in the May 5, 2026 primary {wiki_2026}.

Forums: Both candidates spoke at an Aug. 30, 2026 meet-the-candidates event hosted by the Posey County Farm Bureau {wnin_hd76}. The Evansville NAACP and League of Women Voters of Southwestern Indiana invited all local and state candidates on the ballot to a Sept. 12 forum in Evansville {wnin_forum}; attendance was not reported.

Key differences: On energy costs, Patberg proposes removing the sales tax on residential utility bills and capping how fast investor-owned utilities can raise rates, while McNamara points to the state utility regulator's role and the 2026 utility law (HB 1002) {wnin_hd76}. McNamara supported the 2025 congressional redistricting bill; Patberg's position on it was not reported {wnin_hd76}.

candidates.summary: Logan Patberg is a public school science teacher and Evansville Teachers Association board member making his first run for office {evpl_guide}. He calls energy affordability his top issue {wnin_hd76}.
background: Teaches science in the Evansville-area school district he attended {evpl_guide} {patberg_about}. Serves on the Evansville Teachers Association board and chairs its Advocacy Committee {evpl_guide}.
Describes himself as a lifelong resident of Southwestern Indiana and a union member {patberg_about} {wnin_hd76}. Has not held elected office {evpl_guide}.
path_to_ballot: Filed in early February 2026 {wnin_hd76} {wnin_filing}; unopposed in the May 5, 2026 Democratic primary {wiki_2026}.

items: Proposes eliminating the 7% sales tax on residential utility bills, capping how quickly investor-owned utilities can raise rates (with safety and reliability exceptions) and considering retail energy competition with consumer protections {wnin_hd76}.
Lists keeping energy costs affordable for ratepayers as a priority {patberg_priorities}.
"Data center sales tax extensions should be repealed, because 50 years of a corporate handout is way too long" {wnin_hd76}.
Wants public schools funded at their pre-2008 level and expanded career and technical education; opposes cuts to public higher education {patberg_priorities}.
Says he will "Fight to protect Medicaid/HIP access," expand CHIP (Hoosier Healthwise) for children and lower prescription drug costs {patberg_priorities}.
Supports expanding collective bargaining and workforce development partnerships; says Indiana "needs to have paid leave laws" and more child care capacity {patberg_priorities}.

on_incumbent: Says lawmakers have not answered concerns about jobs, benefits, child care and energy costs well in recent sessions; WNIN reported he did not name McNamara directly on most issues {wnin_hd76}.
plans: Says he wants to give educators, union members and "regular folks" a voice in Indianapolis {wnin_hd76}.
endorsements_finance: No endorsements were listed on his campaign site, and no campaign finance totals were found {patberg_site}.
gaps: No position found on the 2025 property-tax law (SEA 1) or the 2025 congressional redistricting vote.
A WNIN photo caption from the Feb. 3 filing listed Patberg for District 78 and Busby for District 76 in one caption and the reverse in another; the ballot list places Patberg in District 76.

candidates.summary: Wendy McNamara has represented District 76 since 2010, chairs the House Courts and Criminal Code Committee and directs EVSC Early College {caucus_mcnamara}. She cites juvenile justice, anti-trafficking and child-protection laws as her main legislative work {wnin_hd76}.
background: Spent 31 years with the Evansville Vanderburgh School Corporation as a teacher and administrator and created its Early College High School {wnin_hd76}; the caucus lists her as a former teacher, social studies supervisor and assistant principal and adjunct professor {caucus_mcnamara}.
Member of the Justice Reinvestment Advisory Council and a non-voting member of the Indiana Criminal Justice Institute Board of Trustees {evpl_guide}. Lives in Evansville {caucus_mcnamara}.
path_to_ballot: Unopposed in the May 5, 2026 Republican primary {wiki_2026}.

items: Lists mental health, corrections and support for law enforcement among her priorities and says she is drafting bills on alert systems and competency to stand trial {wnin_hd76}.
On HEA 1303: "These predators can do lifelong damage to children" {caucus_csam}.
Says rate-setting rests with the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission and calls HB 1002 "a big step forward," citing relief for lower-income customers and limits on payments {wnin_hd76}.

Says she would again vote for the December 2025 congressional map, citing an estimated $25–30 million a year in federal funding for Posey County and $250–300 million for Vanderburgh County; says constituent responses were mixed {wnin_hd76}.
Plans to expand career and technical education and improve students' transitions to college or work {wnin_hd76}.
Authored the statewide ban on cryptocurrency kiosks, saying it gives the attorney general a path to penalize scammers {caucus_crypto}.

on_incumbent: Is the current officeholder. In response to Patberg's critique on energy costs, she pointed to HB 1002 and the complexity of rate-setting; WNIN reported no direct statements about him {wnin_hd76}.
plans: Says lawmaking requires working across the aisle and that legislators must balance party ideals with constituent needs {wnin_hd76}.
endorsements_finance: No 2026 endorsements or campaign finance totals were found.
gaps: Campaign website appears outdated (news items from 2019); no 2026 issue pages found.
No statement found on the 2025 property-tax law (SEA 1) or data centers.
WNIN notes its interview transcripts were AI-generated with light editing, so quotes may not be exact.
